To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the cost of air pollution control is sensitive to the regulatory approach, that plant relocation can be a very important consideration in the choice of regulatory approach, and that a market for permits can reduce costs significantly.

the estimated cost savings from allowing firms more regulatory flexibility is approximately 30 percent for the hydrocarbon case, that the cost savings are even larger when plant relocation is allowed, and that the cost of the permits is likely to be higher under monopoly than under competitive markets.
the estimated costs of air-polluting emissions are sensitive to the regulatory approach, and that the costs are reduced by allowing firms to trade permits and by allowing plants to relocate.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the effects on the costs of pollution control of (1) the choice of the regulatory instrument (e.g., individual, plant, or marketable permit), and (2) the structure of the market (e.g., monopoly versus competition).
estimating the cost of air pollution control regulation under the alternative regulatory schemes of individual source or plant standards, and marketable permits.
the estimation of the cost of environmental control and the effect of regulatory policy on the cost.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cost of meeting the same standard is lower with a marketable pollution permit system than with a plant standards system.
the marketable permit scheme is superior to the individual source standard approach, and that it is superior to the plant standard scheme when the plant is not allowed to relocate.
the costs of pollution control depend on a number of factors, and that the cost of pollution abatement is sensitive to the specific regulatory approach chosen.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cost of meeting an air-pollution standard is a function of both the stringency of the standard and the regulatory approach adopted.
a marketable permit system is a cost-effective way of controlling hydrocarbon emissions, but the cost savings are reduced by the presence of plant relocation and by monopoly in the pollution market.
the use of plant standards and marketable permits can reduce pollution control costs substantially, but the use of plant relocation and marketable permits may not.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cost estimates for the various control options should be obtained from the regulated firm rather than from the regulator.
the costs of meeting pollution standards can vary widely depending upon the specific regulatory approach.
the choice of regulatory policy has a large effect on the cost of meeting environmental standards, and that this effect can be large enough to be important in policy design and evaluation.
